passage: The queue for the tallest water slide at the park wound up the stairs in the blazing sun, and the sign said you had to be as tall as the red line. Swati, nine, pressed her back against it, stretching her neck. Just over. "Yogesh bhaiya, please! We've done the small one four times. It's so boring." Her cousin looked up at the twisting yellow tube. "It's really fast." "That's the point!" Swati's eyes were shining. They waited forty minutes. At the top her legs shook a little. Then she pushed off and screamed the whole way down, into the pool, and came up spluttering and laughing. "Again! And then the black one!"

grounding: A child begs to try the tallest slide because excitement feels like life and the small slide is boring.

passage: At the Dussehra fair near Pallavi's colony, her father Uday bought tickets for the merry-go-round. Pallavi, ten, sat on a painted horse for one round and climbed off. "Papa, that's for babies. The swing boat! And the dark house! And that new spinning thing!" "You haven't even finished your candy floss." "I'll eat it in the queue." She dragged him from ride to ride, eyes on every new flashing light. The spinning ride made her stomach flip and she shrieked with joy. Then she spotted a stall where you threw rings over bottles. "I've never done that one!" Uday laughed, out of breath. "Is there anything you won't try?" "Boring things," Pallavi said.

qa.q: What could Uday do to help Pallavi enjoy new things without tiring them both out?

qa.q: What is the fair like for Uday?

grounding: A child at a fair wants every new ride and finds the merry-go-round boring; novelty and excitement feel like life to her.

passage: "Ishita didi, I'm bored. Bored bored bored." "You've got a whole shelf of games, Aditi." "I've played them all. A hundred times." Aditi flopped onto her bed. "Can I ride my cycle down the steep lane? No hands?" "No hands, definitely not." "Then what? Everything is boring." Ishita thought. "Okay. New challenge. Build an obstacle course in the hall with cushions. I'll time you." Aditi sat up. "With the stool as a tunnel?" "Sure." "And if I beat two minutes, then I try the lane? With hands?" "With hands, helmet, and me watching." "Deal!" Aditi was already dragging cushions.

qa.q: Which choice by Ishita worked, and why?
qa.a: Ishita offered a new, timed challenge and a safer version of the lane ride, which fed Aditi's hunger for thrill without the no-hands risk.

qa.q: What might Ishita be worried about when Aditi asks for no hands?
qa.a: Ishita is likely worried Aditi could get hurt, which is why she says no firmly but offers something exciting instead.

passage:
I'm Yamini, and last winter we had adventure camp with school. There was a climbing wall, a rope bridge and a zip line over the river.
I couldn't stand in the line. I was jumping up and down. I climbed the small wall first and it was easy, so I begged Sir to let me try the tall one. My brother Vaibhav, who's twelve, said his little sister would get scared. I didn't. My hands were shaking at the top, but I felt so alive.
Then they made us do a slow nature walk. Looking at leaves! I nearly died of boredom. I'd rather have a scraped knee than that.
Next camp I want to try the zip line twice.

qa.a: The small wall.

qa.a: Her hands were shaking, but she felt so alive and thrilled to have done something new and challenging.

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help a child like Yamini on the nature walk?
qa.a: A teacher could turn the walk into a challenge, like a hunt for unusual leaves, so her love of excitement is used safely instead of fighting boredom.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt watching his sister climb the tall wall?
qa.a: He might have been surprised and a little impressed, since he had said she would get scared.

grounding: It shows a child who begs to try the tallest climbing wall and every new challenge, for whom excitement feels like life and boredom feels worse than a little risk.

passage:
Summer camp note, Wednesday. Disha, activities lead.
Every morning Anand (9) asks, "What's new today?" He tried every game in the first hour and wanted to know which was hardest. At the water park he went straight to the tallest slide, stretching up to meet the height line, and after three rides asked to go head first.
Quiet activities are hard for him. In painting hour he lay on the floor and groaned, "This is so boring I might explode." He isn't being rude; excitement seems to be what makes him feel awake.
I said no to head first. Instead I had him time the others on the obstacle course, then try to beat his own best. He stayed focused for forty minutes.
Next: a new challenge for him each day, with clear safety limits.

qa.q: What does Anand ask every morning?
qa.a: What's new today?

qa.q: What does Anand's comment about exploding from boredom show about him?
qa.a: It shows that quiet, familiar tasks feel almost unbearable to him, because new challenges are what make him feel awake and alive.

qa.q: Which of Disha's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Turning down the head-first slide but giving him a timed obstacle challenge worked, because it fed his need for thrill within safe limits.

qa.q: How might the other children see Anand during the painting hour?
qa.a: They might find his groaning and lying on the floor funny or annoying, not realising how hard quiet activities are for him.

grounding: It shows a child who craves every new game and the tallest slide, for whom boredom feels worse than risk, and an adult who channels it into safe challenges.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage:
Shalini, you're begging your mother to let you try the giant swing at the fair. Let me tell you about me at nine.
I'm Vijay, your Dada, and I had to try everything new. The tallest slide at the mela. The first ride on a neighbour's cycle. Sitting still bored me more than a scraped knee ever hurt.
One summer I climbed the big tamarind tree higher than anyone. I slipped on the way down and scraped my whole leg.
My father didn't forbid me. He said, "Climb, but learn how." He showed me which branches held, how to keep three hands and feet on the tree. That made climbing more exciting, not less.
So try the swing. Hold the bar tight, and let your mother watch.

qa.q: What tree did young Vijay climb?
qa.a: The big tamarind tree.

qa.q: What was young Vijay feeling when sitting still?
qa.a: He felt bored and restless, finding stillness worse than a scraped knee.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vijay's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: His father teaching him how to climb safely was the turning point, because it let him keep the thrill while learning to manage the risk.

qa.q: How might Vijay's father have felt seeing the scraped leg?
qa.a: He was probably worried but calm, choosing to teach rather than forbid.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, he craved new thrills and learned safer ways to enjoy them.

passage:
The water park closed at five, the queues were long, and Ganga had one hour left and a headache. But Yogesh, eight, was pulling her hand towards the tallest slide.
"That one, Amma! Please! I've done all the small ones five times!"
"It's very high, Yogesh."
"The small ones are boring. I want the big one!"
They queued for thirty minutes in the sun. At the top, the lifeguard measured Yogesh against the height board. He was tall enough, just.
Ganga watched from below, heart thumping. He came shooting out of the tunnel with a scream that turned into laughter, water everywhere.
"AGAIN!" he shouted, before he'd even stood up.
Ganga checked the clock: twenty minutes. "Once more. Then home."
He was already running.

qa.q: How long did they queue for the tallest slide?
qa.a: Thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he came out of the tunnel?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and joyful, bursting with excitement to go again.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that kept the thrill safe?
qa.a: She queued with him, let the lifeguard check his height and watched from below, allowing the new challenge within safe limits.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel watching from below?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with her heart thumping, while he enjoyed the excitement.

grounding: It shows a child begging to try the tallest slide because excitement feels like life and boredom feels worse.

passage:
A new trampoline park had opened at the Andheri mall, and Suraj, ten, had talked of nothing else for a week.
"Can we go? Please? I'll do my homework on the bus."
His sister Rajni, sixteen, sighed. "You've been to the park, the pool, the cricket nets, all this month."
"But those are old! This is new!"
She took him on Saturday. Inside, Suraj didn't go to the small trampolines. He went straight to the foam pit and the high wall.
The staff made everyone wear grip socks and listen to the safety rules, while Suraj bounced from foot to foot.
Then he jumped, flipped halfway, landed in the foam and came up shouting with joy.
"Rajni! It's the BEST!"
Going home, he asked about the climbing wall in Thane.

qa.q: What did the staff make everyone wear?
qa.a: Grip socks.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he came up from the foam?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and joyful, excited by the new challenge.

qa.q: How could Rajni help Suraj enjoy new thrills safely?
qa.a: She could keep taking him to places with safety rules and staff, and help him wait for his turn to listen to the rules first.

qa.q: How does Rajni seem to see Suraj's constant wish for new things?
qa.a: She seems a little tired of it, but she still takes him and watches him enjoy it.

grounding: It shows a child craving new, exciting activities, where boredom feels worse than a little risk.

passage:
I'm Leela and I'm ten. Last summer at my Nani's village I nearly died of boredom. There was nothing new. Same mango tree, same well, same cows.
So I made up games. I tried climbing to the top branch of the mango tree. I tried jumping over the stream at its widest point. My cousin Rehana said I was mad.
"Why can't you just sit and play carrom?"
"Carrom is boring! I want to feel my heart go boom!"
When I fell in the stream, Nani pulled me out and said, "At least tell me before your next adventure." So I did. The next one was riding the bullock cart with the farmer, holding the rope, with Nani waving.
Best day of the whole summer.

qa.q: Where did Leela spend last summer?
qa.a: At Nani's village.

qa.q: What does Leela feel that makes climbing and jumping so tempting?
qa.a: Leela feels bored when nothing is new and craves excitement, wanting to 'feel my heart go boom'.

qa.q: How did Nani handle Leela's love of adventure?
qa.a: Nani didn't ban it, but asked Leela to tell her first, so Leela could have thrills with an adult knowing and nearby.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Leela's adventures?
qa.a: Rehana thinks Leela is mad and prefers calm games like carrom.

grounding: A child finds the familiar boring and seeks thrills like climbing and jumping, feeling excitement is life itself.

passage:
Swimming club coach's note, Wednesday

Nirmala, eleven, has now tried every activity at the club in two months: diving board, relay, water polo, even synchronised swimming. Each time, she is thrilled for a week and then says, "It's boring now."
Today she asked to jump from the highest board, which is not allowed at her level. When I said no, she argued: "But I need something new, or I'll go crazy!" Francis, the lifeguard, laughed and said she reminded him of himself.
I've offered her the diving training programme, with proper supervision, so she has a real challenge with safety. She jumped around the pool deck when I told her.

qa.q: What activities has Nirmala tried at the club?
qa.a: The diving board, relay, water polo and synchronised swimming.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's 'I'll go crazy!' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was restless and eager, feeling that boredom is worse than risk, and craving a new challenge.

qa.q: Why was offering the diving training programme a good step?
qa.a: It gives Nirmala real challenge and excitement with proper supervision, instead of just saying no.

qa.q: How does Francis see Nirmala?
qa.a: Francis finds her funny and familiar, saying she reminds him of himself.

grounding: A coach notes a child who craves novelty, gets bored quickly and seeks bigger thrills, and offers a supervised challenge.

passage: Dear Diary, Dussehra fair day!!! Ganga here, too excited to sleep. I begged Lakshmi Akka to take me on the tallest slide, the yellow one that goes round and round, and she said, 'Only if the man checks your height.' I stood on my toes. I PASSED. My tummy flipped all the way down and I screamed and then I wanted to go AGAIN. Then I tried the bumper cars, the mirror house, and I asked for the ride that spins you upside down, which Akka said no to, so I did the camel ride instead. Boring. subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: The mustard fields around Rampura were yellow to the horizon, and Sarika had been bored for three whole days of winter holidays. She had counted the buffaloes, climbed the same neem, and swung on the same tyre till it felt like homework. So when Yusuf, the tailor's son from next door, came pedalling his tall black bicycle along the canal road, she ran after him. 'Teach me! Down the slope, the steep one!' 'You'll fly into the canal.' 'Anything is better than the tyre. Please!' Yusuf laughed. 'Flat road first. If you can stop without falling, then the slope, and I run beside you.' Sarika wobbled, crashed into a mustard row, laughed, and got straight back on. By sunset she was shrieking down the slope, Yusuf panting behind.

qa.q: What had Sarika swung on until it felt like homework?
qa.a: The same tyre.

qa.q: Why did Sarika beg to go down the steep slope?
qa.a: She was desperately bored and craved excitement; a little risk felt far better to her than another day on the tyre.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's plan get right?
qa.a: He didn't crush Sarika's thirst for thrills; he made it safer with the flat road first and running beside her on the slope.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel running behind Sarika at sunset?
qa.a: Yusuf is probably tired and a little nervous, but also amused and proud of how fast she learned.

grounding: In a winter village a girl who finds sameness unbearable begs to try a steep bicycle slope.

passage: The winter festival in their Hokkaido town had ice slides taller than houses, and Hiroshi wanted every one. After the small slide twice and the snow maze once, he was hopping on the spot. 'The big one, Kaito! The one with the curve!' Kaito, his older brother, looked at the queue and the steep blue ice. 'Mum said the small ones.' 'The small ones are for babies. I'm going to die of boredom.' 'You'll bump your head, more like.' Hiroshi tugged his brother's glove. 'I'll wear the helmet they give out. And I'll sit, not lie down.' Kaito read the sign by the steps: helmets required, young children with an older companion. He sighed. 'Fine. I'm right behind you.' At the bottom Hiroshi's cheeks were pink, and he was already pointing at the snow rafting.

qa.a: Helmets required, young children with an older companion.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi's hopping on the spot suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was restless and excited, eager for something bigger than the small slides he now found boring.

qa.q: What could Mum do at home to feed Hiroshi's craving for thrills safely?
qa.a: She could plan new, safe challenges, like a climbing class or a new sport, so Hiroshi gets excitement without chasing risky ones.

qa.q: What is it like for Kaito to be in charge of Hiroshi at the festival?
qa.a: Kaito is caught between Mum's rule and his brother's pleading; feeling responsible, he checks the sign and goes right behind him.

grounding: At a winter festival abroad a boy begs for the tallest ice slide and every new game, finding boredom worse than risk.

passage:
The sports club's winter carnival had a new climbing wall, three storeys of coloured holds, and Ayesha had spotted it from the gate.
"Himani Ma'am, please, please can I go first?" She was already bouncing on her toes.
"It's the tallest one. Are you sure? The small wall is open too."
"The small wall is for babies. I did it last year. It's so boring." Ayesha tugged at her harness strap. "Please! What if I can reach the top?"
Himani Ma'am checked the harness twice and clipped the rope. Ayesha scrambled up, knees scraping, heart racing, and slapped the bell at the top. It rang across the whole club.
"Next!" she shouted down. "What's next?"

qa.a: Three storeys of coloured holds.

qa.q: Why does Ayesha call the small wall boring?
qa.a: She feels bored by what she has already done and excited by anything new and hard, so the tallest wall feels far more alive than the safe one.

qa.q: How did Himani Ma'am balance Ayesha's thirst for thrills with safety?
qa.a: She checked the harness twice and clipped the rope, letting Ayesha take the challenge with protection in place.

qa.q: How might Himani Ma'am feel hearing Ayesha shout "What's next?"
qa.a: Himani Ma'am probably feels amused and a little tired, seeing that one thrill only makes Ayesha hungry for the next.

grounding: A child begs to climb the tallest wall because anything familiar feels boring and new challenges feel thrilling.
